content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors claim a well-performed network compression training scheme is proposed, where the original network and the targeted compression one are trained together, thus achieves better performance compared with the conventional network compression methods.
content.main_review:
There are numerous weakness with this paper, only very small part of them are listed here:

1. The writting should be improved. Currently, the writing is not on the level of academic papers.

2. Since the authors claim the outputs of the networks as 'possiblities', it should be clarified that the experiments are setted as classification tasks. However, this clarification is missed, thus leads to confusion.

3. The authors claim 'good teachers are lifelong learners'. However, is there any solution disigned for the overfitting problem in the teacher network? Is the lifelong learning for new knowledge or simply the pre-defined knowledge? Without clear definition of these two terms, this claim may not correct.

4. In the Adjoined Networks section, the compression parameter M is fixed, which may leads to poor generalizability.

5. The authors claim 'This also has a regularizing effect as it forces the network to learn from a smaller set of parameters' and list this effect as a benefit for network compression. However, in order to prove this statement, an experiment for comparing the original network and a maksed network should be conducted (not includes the compression operation).

6. In the regularization term \lambda(t), the variable t is hyper-parameter dependent, which may not stable and functional enough when the totoal_number_of_epochs are set as small number.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the poor writing quality, problemtic setting, unstable performance for this paper, it cannot be accepted as any academical publication.

content.title: Response to reviewer 4
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for taking the time to go through the paper and provide us with his/her feedback. Please find our responses below. 
***
### Writing
The reviewer mentions that the writing could be improved. We thank the reviewer for this comment. If the reviewer could provide some details on the aspects that he/she found not at the level of an academic publication that we would be very useful to us and would also lend more credibility to the feedback.
***
### Matrix $M$
It seems that the reviewer has misunderstood why the parameter $M$ was introduced in the architecture design. After the learning finishes, the structure of $M$ allows us to directly prune away the all-zero filters.This helps us translate the parameter savings to speed-ups in inference time. It would be helpful if the reviewer could provided reasons as to why/how fixing $M$ may lead to poor generalization. 
***
### Regularization behaviour
It seems that the reviewer has missed the experiments in Section 7.4 where we had provided experimental results of the regularization behaviour of our approach on two datasets (ImageNet and CIFAR-100). It also appears that the reviewer missed Section 6 that had theoretical justification for the regularization behaviour of adjoint training. In the current draft, we have added even more experiments about the same. Please refer to the common response (item #1)
***
### $\lambda(t)$
We agree with the reviewer that this can happen when training for a very small number of epochs for some choices of lambda. However, in the adjoined training paradigm, we are training both the teacher and the student together from scratch. As such, we typically train for a high number of epochs. In cases, when it is required to train for a small number of epochs, using $\lambda(t) = c$ (constant) would resolve the issues raised by the reviewer.   
***
We make the following requests to the reviewer. Kindly provide more justification for the comments. Please avoid spelling and common grammatical mistakes in the reviews.
* “writting” -> “writing”
* “may not stable” -> “may not be stable”
* “is there any solution disigned” -> “is there any solution designed”
* “problemtic setting” -> “problematic setting”
* “as any academical publication.”  -> “as an academic publication”

display_title: Official Review of Paper1908 by Reviewer jxrL

content.summary_of_the_paper: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been achieving state of the art performance in various tasks, but such models tend to be overparameterized and difficult to be deployed on edge devices such as mobile phones and IoT devices. To address the challenges, this paper proposes Adjoined Networks (ANs) and Differentiable Adjoined Networks (DANs). AN is a novel training framework inspired from knowledge distillation, which trains larger and smaller networks (base and compressed models respectively) jointly, with a new loss function specifically for this new framework. DAN searches for some of the hyperparameters in ANs, including choices of  pre-defined subnetwork architectures.  Using the CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets, the authors empirically demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves prediction performance comparable to more complex models while saving inference cost (model size and GFLOPs).
content.main_review:
**Strengths:**
1. This paper works on an important problem that it is difficult to deploy and use powerful deep neural models due to their model size. While there are a lot of studies addressing this problem such as knowledge distillation and model pruning with software/hardware support, the authors proposed a unique solution that trains larger and smaller models jointly. Different from deep mutual learning (DML), which trains two separate student models jointly, their proposed AN (and DAN) models share some of the trainable layers (e.g., a compressed model uses a subset of the larger base model). Compared to DML, the property that “shares trainable layers shared between teacher (base) and student (compressed) models” looks like a new paradigm and could reduce 1) training cost in terms of model size on memory and 2) design cost for student model as the student in this paradigm looks pruned version of the teacher.

2. Using the CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets, this paper performed a sufficient amount of experiments to discuss the effectiveness of their proposed approach. The experiments involve comparisons not only to knowledge distillation methods, but also to model pruning approaches. Besides the main experiments, the authors performed ablation studies to discuss the effects of different model size and regularization by their proposed approach.

3. While addressing the challenging task, the approaches themselves look relatively simple and straightforward. e.g., the new loss function is an extension of knowledge distillation loss by Hinton et al. (2015). I think this should be a positive aspect as the authors did not unnecessarily make the approach overcomplex and achieving the goal by the simple approach should be appreciated in the research communities.

4. For reproducibility of this work, the authors provide details of their hyperparameter choices (image transforms, data augmentation, number of epochs, optimizer, learning rate adjustment, and more) besides their source code (as part of supplementary material). Due to limited access to computing resources, I did not run their code, but the combination of the description about hyperparameters and source code look good enough to attempt to reproduce their experimental results.


**Weaknesses:**
1. Given that the effectiveness of the authors’ proposed approach is supported by their experimental results, there are some concerns in models the authors chose for numerical comparison, specifically for CIFAR-100 datasets.

ResNet-18, -50 and DenseNet-121 were originally designed for higher-resolution images (e.g., 224x224) and a more complex task, which is the ImageNet dataset.  Though many of experimental results for CIFAR-100 are based on the models, these specific models have not been well benchmarked for CIFAR-100 in prior studies, and I suspect that the authors pruned some layers in the models to work with smaller images (32x32).

Suggestion: To make the experimental results on CIFAR dataset convincing (for a fair comparison), I would suggest ResNet and DenseNet models designed and validated for CIFAR datasets in their original papers such as ResNet-20, -32, -44, -56, and -110 and DenseNet-BC (k=12, 24, 40).
Also, why did the authors build a new model, ResNet-100 instead of using ResNet-101 validated for the ImageNet dataset in the original paper?

If the authors could apply such a quantization technique to their proposed method using their model weights pretrained on ImageNet as a starting point and still preserve the comparable accuracy with INT8 version, this paper can be stronger.
https://github.com/pytorch/vision/tree/master/references/classification


2. While this paper proposes both the Adjoined Network and Differentiable Adjoined Network losses (Eqs. 3 and 6), the essential difference between these two loss functions look unclear.

The authors defined Eq. 6 by adding γ n_f to Eq. 3 where γ is a balancing factor (hyperparameter) and n_f is the total number of floating point operations or FLOPs of the network. However, the extra term (γ n_f) is not differentiable with respect to the input x, thus will be ignored when computing gradients of model parameters. In other words, Eq. 6 would be essentially the same as Eq. 3 as a loss function.

Suggestion: If the authors used Eq. 6 as metric for model selection i.e., to choose which version of their (D)AN models should be used for evaluation, it should be re-formulated in a different way and referred to as an evaluation metric (for model selection) rather than a loss function optimized by SGD/Adam.

3. Similarly, the value of γ for the constant term n_f is set to e^-15 or e^-19, which is prohibitively small, thus the contribution by Eq. 6 is not clear from the current experimental results, compared to that by Eq. 3. Did the authors use Eq. 6 just as a metric for search (model selection)? 

Suggestion: To show the importance of Eq. 6., I’d suggest the authors use γ=0 to obtain new results.

4. This is not critical, but a suggestion to strengthen this work. As the authors stated “In this paper, our focus is to compress existing architectures while ensuring inference time speedups as well as maintaining prediction accuracy.”, adding numerical comparison to (even simple) quantization techniques would make this paper stronger.
For instance,  “DAN achieves ResNet-50 level accuracy on ImageNet with 3.8× fewer parameters and 2.2× fewer FLOPs.” can be achieved by INT8 quantized ResNet-50 (75.9% accuracy for ImageNet), that has the same number of parameters as ResNet-50 but saves 75% in model size by 32-bit float -> 8-bit int.
https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/models.html#quantized-models

If the authors could apply such a quantization technique to their proposed method using their model weights pretrained on ImageNet as a starting point and still preserve the comparable accuracy with INT8 version, this paper can be stronger.
https://github.com/pytorch/vision/tree/master/references/classification


**Typos:**
There are repeated typos I found in this paper:
- “Differentiable Adjoined Networks (DAN)” -> “Differentiable Adjoined Networks (DANs)”
- “Adjoined Networks (AN)” -> “Adjoined Networks (ANs)”
- “in the supplementary .” -> “in the supplementary material.”
- “in supplementary .” -> “in the supplementary material.”
- “Table 1 and Figure 1 compares” -> “Table 1 and Figure 1 compare”

The references section is incomplete. Many entries miss the venues and/or contain wrong information.
e.g., “Kim et al. (2020)” -> “Kim et al. (2018)”. The factor transfer paper was published in NeurIPS 2018.

The following abbreviations/acronyms should be consistent and corrected:
- “Eq.” vs. “Eqn.”
- “Def.” vs. “Defn.”
- “For eg.,” -> “For example,”

**Minor:**
- Do rows in “first c_out / alpha rows” in page 4 refer to channels/filters? If so, either channels or filters would be more intuitive.
- What do “stem layers” in page 7 mean?
- Do “res-blocks” in page 7 mean residual blocks? If so, I’d suggest you write so.
- What does “a super-net” in page 6 mean?
- It is not clear if Section 6 is necessary as part of the main content since it looks isolated and not well connected to the neighboring sections.
- What is a white box at the end of “Proof sketch” ?
- How did the authors define GFLOPs? Some papers refer to only those of convolution and linear layers as FLOPs, thus should be clarified.
- I would suggest the authors provide more instructions (+ exact commands) to reproduce the experimental results reported in this work.
- The considered baseline KD methods look a little bit old. For image classification, I would suggest the prime-aware adaptive distillation (PAD) and knowledge review (KR) as additional baselines besides the methods (at least for future studies):
  - Zhang et al. "Prime-Aware Adaptive Distillation" @ ECCV 2020  
  - Chen et al. "Distilling Knowledge via Knowledge Review" @ CVPR 2021
  - I found both the implementations available in torchdistill https://github.com/yoshitomo-matsubara/torchdistill
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper performed a sufficient amount of experiments with model pruning and knowledge distillation baselines and showed comparable model accuracy with compressed model size and reduced flops. I also found some novelty in the framework (e.g., training larger and smaller models jointly, time-dependent loss term).
As described above, my main concerns are models for the CIFAR-100 dataset, numerical comparison to quantization (as the goal is the same as this paper),  and essential differences between AN and DAN given that the new term in DAN is constant and will be ignored when computing gradients.

Overall, I’m inclined to suggest rejection.  I left many concerns and small questions above. If the authors could resolve them, I’d be happy to increase my score. The key issues are
1. inappropriate model choices for numerical comparison (mostly for CIFAR-100),
2. potentially critical issue in the loss function for DAN,
3. importance of the loss function for DAN compared to that for AN, and
4. (optional) comparison with simple quantization techniques that could easily achieve the objective set in this paper. 

[EDIT after discussions]
Now I’m inclined to suggest acceptance given that some of the main concerns above were resolved by the authors' clarifications.

content.title: Response to reviewer 3
content.comment:
We would really like to thank the reviewer for reading the paper in great detail for the numerous insightful comments and suggestions. We have addressed them and provide our answers below. We hope that the reviewer will re-consider the evaluation in light of responses.
***
### 1. Experiments
We would like to thank the reviewer for pointing out that it makes more sense to compare our approach on architectures like ResNet-20,-32,-44,-56 and -110 when considering datasets like CIFAR-10. In light of these comments, we carried out extensive experiments involving both compression and knowledge distillation on this dataset. Please refer to the common response (item #1) for further details on the evaluation. Our experiments show that our approach beats the state-of-the-art results for both compression and knowledge distillation on many of these smaller models. 
***
### 2 and 3. Question about the DAN loss function
The reviewer raised some questions related to the DAN loss function. We thank the reviewer for raising this question. In the presentation in the paper, it seemed that $n_f$ is constant and hence the term $\gamma n_f$  is constant and has no effect on the optimization process. We have added a clarification to this. Please refer to the common response (item #2). We have also added the same details in the paper (Section 5). Hopefully, this should resolve the questions and confusion around both the terms $n_f$ and the multiplication factor $\gamma$ and why Eqns. 3 and 6 are not equivalent for $\gamma \neq 0$ and why we use a low value for $\gamma$.
***
### 4. Relation to quantization
We thank the reviewer for the suggestion of combining quantization with our current approach. The reviewer correctly points out that quantization alone can often give benefits like 2-3x reduction in size and compute. We would like to say that the technique presented in this paper is quantization friendly. That is, we can combine our approach with INT8 quantization to achieve a further 2-3x improvements. Thus, it is complementary to the technique presented. In this paper, our goal was to reduce the number of effective parameters in the model and hence we did not focus as much on combining our approach with integer quantization. We have identified this as an area of future work.  
***
### Clarifications 
* We have addressed the typos raised by the reviewer like in the paper. Like replacing res-blocks by residual blocks, moving section 6 to the supplementary, adding more instructions for running our code, comparing against some of the suggested works.
* The term super-net was meant to convey that dan can be thought of as an architecture that contains all the sub-architectures in it (Fig 3). We have removed this and modified the discussion in Section 5 to convey these ideas more precisely. 
* Layers before the residual blocks are called stem layers.
* We calculate FLOPs for all layers including batchnorm, relu, pooling layers etc

replying_to: Replying to Thank you for the response, but I need further clarifications

content.title: Further Clarifications
content.comment:
Again, we thank the reviewer for his comments and happy to provide further clarifications. 

### 1. Hyper-parameter tuning
For the CIFAR-10 and -100 datasets, our hyper-parameter tuning approach is the following. Out of the 50k train set, we randomly select 40k and mark it for training and 10k for validation. We then select the hyper-parameters that have maximum accuracy on the validation set. We then train the model on the full 50k train set and report the numbers on the test set. For baseline (for example accuracy of the CIFAR-10 when trained in the standard fashion) we use the numbers reported in the literature.  

### 2. Clarifications around $n_f$ or $(\eta_1, \ldots, \eta_m)$
Lets revisit our optimization problem. The goal of the optimization is the following $$\min_{\text{params}, \eta} \enspace \sum_{(x, y)}  L_1(y, p(x), q(x))  + n_f (\eta) $$ where $L_1$ is as in Eqn. 3 and $(x, y)$ denotes a labelled training example ($x$ is the features and $y$ is the corresponding label). Note that $p$ and $q$ are the outputs of the large and small networks and hence depend upon the parameters of the model `params`.  If $p(x), q(x)$ were independent of the term $\eta$ then the above optimization problem could be broken down into two independent optimization problems as the abve equation would be equivalent to $$\min_{\text{params}} \enspace \sum_{(x, y)}  L_1(y, p(x), q(x))  +  \min_{\eta} n_f (\eta) $$
In this case, the reviewer is correct in arguing that the values of $\eta$ will be ignored when computing the gradient updates for the parameters as the two are independent problems. However, the problem with this analysis is that the term $q(x)$ is not independent of $\eta$ in the DAN formulation. While the network output $p(x)$ is the same as before; the term $q(x)$ now depends upon both the `params` and $\eta$. To see why this is case, we request the reviewer to please revisit the paragraphs between Defns 2 and 3. The whole idea is that the output $z$ of a DAN convolution layer $$z = \sum_{i=1}^{m}   g(\eta)_i  \enspace z_i $$ is a weighted sum of the output of the $z_i$'s that correspond to the different values of $\alpha$. Thus, the optimization problem should be viewed as

$$\min_{\text{params}, \eta} \enspace \sum_{(x, y)}  L_1(y, p(x; \text{params}), q(x; \text{params}, \eta))  + n_f (\eta) $$
Thus, in this optimization problem the gradient updates for the model parameters will not be independent of $\eta$.  
In the paper, we write this whole optimization problem as minimizing the loss function $L_1(y, p, q)  + n_f (\eta) $ for brevity which might have lead to the confusion. 

### 3. Tuning $\gamma$
We have added an ablation study in the supplementary where we tune the value of the parameter $\gamma$. As the reviewer had anticipated, this experiment (Table 16 in the supplementary) shows that for low values of $\gamma$, DAN prefers networks with low values of alpha. This is reflected in the number of flops and parameters of the selected architecture. As $\gamma$ grows, DAN learning prefers smaller architectures. Thus, $\gamma$ is an regularization parameter.

content.title: Increased score
content.comment:
I thank the authors for the further clarifications.
Given that some of my main concerns were resolved, I increased my score.

Lastly, I'd suggest that the authors describe their answers to "1. Hyper-parameter tuning" and "3. Tuning $\gamma$" either in the main paper or supplementary material. Specifically, Table 16 seems to have never been mentioned in the paper/supplementary material.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a novel framework for distilling knowledge and compressing a student network. The authors propose the concept of Adjoined Networks (AN) where the student and the teacher network have some common layer-wise trainable parameters and are trained together. Building on this concept, the authors also propose Differentiable Adjoined Networks (DAN)  that augments AN by using NAS which helps in the layer-wise learning of compression parameter alpha for the student network. The proposed framework is tested on ResNet50 architecture as a teacher and on the task of image classification on ImageNet.
content.main_review:
Strength:
The idea of Adjoined Networks is exciting and novel. The evaluation performed showcases that the proposed framework can significantly reduce the space-time complexity of the student network while achieving better results than other relevant works.

Weakness:
1. The authors compare their work with a minimal set of results in the area of network pruning and knowledge distillation. Therefore, the authors should compare with more works such as deep mutual learning and other works where intermediate features are used for distillation.

2. The authors used binary matrices M with a particular structure. Did the authors also tried other structures where the whole matrix M consists of binary values (with uniform and non uniform distribution) and not just few rows? I think that such structure will also save computation and parameters, although the number of channels will remain. I agree that, in that case, the design of alpha will change, but the authors can comment on this.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I am positive about the paper, however, there is a need to extend the evaluation. The area of network pruning and knowledge distillation is vast, so minimal comparison does not give the complete picture of where this method stands.

content.title: Response to reviewer 2
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for his comments on the paper. Below, we address the comments raised by the reviewer. 
***
### 1. Experiments
We have added several new experiments and comparisons. Please refer to the common response section (Item #1) for detailed comments on how we have addressed this concern. 
**
### 2. Questions about the mask matrix
The reviewer correctly points that our mask matrix M has a particular structure. The choice of this structure is intentional. After the learning finishes, the structure of M allows us to directly prune away the all-zero filters.This helps us translate the parameter savings to speed-ups in inference time. Another reasonable choice (also suggested by the reviewer) is that we choose a mask matrix M according to a distribution (say all the entries from a distribution that samples zero with probability p and one with probability 1-p). By tuning the value of the parameter p, we could control the sparsity and achieve reduction in the number of parameters. We conducted an ablation study where we vary the value of the parameter p and compare the performance of both the large teacher model and the small student model (trained adjointly with the unstructured mask matrix M) against the performance of the large and small models trained adjointly with a structured mask matrix M’ (corresponding to alpha = 2). For p=0.5, both the small and large adjoined models had slightly worse (0.1-0.5%) performance than their structured counterparts. We refer the reviewer to Table 15 for detailed results of our evaluation and thank him/her for suggesting this experiment.

Another reason for preferring the structured mask matrix has to do with inference speeds. To get speed-ups using the un-structured matrix at test time would probably require specialized hardware or support for sparse multiplications.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1908 by Reviewer UxeW

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper discusses an approach to train a teacher and student model together to improve distillation. In addition, it describes a technique called Differentiable Adjoint Networks which learns a scaling parameter for each layer, alpha, that determines the number of filters in each convolutional layer in the student model.

These methods are evaluated on standard image classification benchmarks such as ImageNet and CIFAR-100 with ResNet and DenseNet. architectures.
content.main_review:
**Strengths:**
1. Clarity

The clarity of the paper is good and it contains relevant details about the training procedure.

2. Baselines


The knowledge distillation baselines used are useful in comparing this approach with other existing alternatives.

**Weaknesses:**

1. Novelty

The proposed method is a combination of previously explored ideas such as feature sharing, structure learning and co-distillation/online distillation and therefore lacks novelty.

Co-distillation/Online distillation: 
Deep Mutual Learning by Zhang et. al (CVPR 2018) - cited
Online Knowledge Distillation via Collaborative Learning by Guo et. al (CVPR 2020)

Structured pruning:
Slimmable Networks by Yu et. al. (ICLR 2019) - cited
Universally Slimmable Networks and Improved Training Techniques Yu et. al. (ICCV 2019)


2. Correctness

In Definition 2 (Differentiable Adjoined loss), the new term added nf doesn't seem like a differentiable term and it is unclear how this is useful to add to the loss function. More details on the how nf is computed and affects training are needed.

3. Experimental evaluation

While the experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-100 provide some evidence towards the performance of the approach, evaluations on additional datasets and tasks would strengthen the empirical evidence of the approach.

4. Organization

The organization of table 3 could be improved. In the ImageNet section, the DAN-100 results are grouped with ResNet-50 instead of being grouped with the ResNet-100 base model. And in the CIFAR-100 section, a result is provided for DAN-100 without its corresponding base model.

**Minor notes:**
- Section 4 is titled: 4 ONE-SHOT REGULARIZATION AND COMPRESSION
However, the term one-shot is usually used when describing a method that learns from a small number of training examples. Overloading this term could cause confusion to the reader.
- The statement at the end of section 6: "Thus, adjoined loss "encourages" such parameters to not change by a lot thereby enabling compression" needs more elaboration.
- Regarding the loss in definition 1, why was groundtruth only used to train the teacher and not the student? It seems natural to train the student with available groundtruth in a model compression setting.
- The semantics of alpha is inconsistent between Section 1 and the rest of the paper. Alpha is said to be "1/4 or 1/2" in the introduction while it is a whole number in the rest of the paper.
- The point about additional regularization of the teacher model seems a bit out of place to the main goal of model compression and makes the narrative a bit confusing. The motivation for why this is useful could be elaborated upon more if it is an important result.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, the paper is clearly written and contributes an approach to knowledge distillation that is supported by some empirical evidence.
However it lacks novelty and there are several areas that the paper could be improved in terms of organization and additional details.

content.title: Response to reviewer 1
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for his comments on the paper. Below, we address all the points raised by the reviewer. We hope that the reviewer will reconsider the evaluation in light of our responses.
***
### 1. Novelty 
The reviewer points out that the paper combines ideas in structure learning, feature sharing  and knowledge distillation. We would like to respectfully disagree with the reviewer that combining ideas as done in the paper is not novel. While we have tried to stay modest in our claims in the paper and not over-sell our results (as is the trend these days); our experimental results (on ImageNet and updated results on CIFAR-10) do demonstrate that we outperform the current state-of-the art results on these datasets for many architectures (including ResNet-50, -20, -32, -44, -56, -110) on both compression and knowledge distillation tasks.

The reviewer correctly points out some similarities to the DML paper that jointly trains a cohort of students together. However, there are many important differences. (1) Training the teacher and the student jointly reduces the cost of training (both in terms of memory and model size). (2) This also makes it very easy to choose/design a new student architecture. A compressed architecture can be easily selected by choosing a different value of alpha (done by altering the hyper-parameter alpha in the implementation) allowing the user to easily choose between the different student models offering size-accuracy trade-offs. The same sentiment was also offered by Reviewer 3. (3) We have also augmented our approach with architecture search. (4) We also provide theoretical justification (regularization behaviour) for some aspects of our approach. (5) Furthermore, we compare our approach exhaustively against DML, KDCL and Slimmable Networks. Tables 1, 2 and 14 show that our method outperforms both these methods on both compression and knowledge distillation tasks; on different models (ResNet-50, ResNet-20 , 32 etc) on different datasets like CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet showing the superiority of the proposed method.
***
### 2. Correctness
We thank the reviewer for pointing out that the details of n_f computation should be clarified for better understanding. Please refer to our common response section (item #2). We have also added the same details in the paper (Section 5).
***
### 3. Experiments 
We have added several new experiments. Please refer to the common response section (item #1)
***
### 4. Organization 
We thank the reviewer for pointing out the grouping in one of the tables. We have made that edit.
***
### Minor notes:
* Changed the title for Section 4 to remove the term one-shot.
* Our goal/intuition was to train the teacher using the ground truth and let the teacher distill that information to the student. In this way, the output of the teacher acts as soft labels for the students. While it is definitely possible to train the students also with soft labels; in our experiments we found that using soft labels generally gave better results. 
* Thanks for pointing out the inconsistency. We have changed it to say alpha = 2, 4 etc throughout.
* Moved the theoretical discussion about regularization to the appendix.

replying_to: Replying to Adjoined Networks: A Training Paradigm with Applications to Network Compression

content.title: Common response to all reviewers
content.comment:
We would like to thank all the reviewers for their insightful comments and suggestions on helping improve the results presented in this paper. In this section, we address two issues that were raised by multiple reviewers. Below, we address some of the common concerns that were raised by multiple reviewers. We also provide individual responses to all the reviewer comments in the respective sections.  
***

### 1. Experiments on more datasets and/or more models- (Raised by reviewers 1, 2, 3 and 4)

This was a common concern raised by multiple reviewers and we would like to thank the reviewers for pointing this out as well as providing suggestions about datasets and models. We would especially like to thank reviewer 3 for suggesting experiments on the CIFAR-10 dataset. 

We have added several experiments to strengthen the empirical evidence of our approach. In the current version of the paper, we have provided compression results on ImageNet for ResNet-50 (Tables 1, 3); on CIFAR-100 for ResNet-18,-50(Tables 6,7) and Densenet-121(Table 8); on CIFAR-10 for ResNet-20,-32,-44,-56,-110 (Table 3). On each of these datasets, we compare (Table 1, 12, 13,  Figure 1, 4, 8) against the current state-of-the-art methods (according to our knowledge) and outperform (on several datasets) or are competitive with (on some datasets) these methods. 
In the current version of the paper, we have conducted knowledge distillation experiments on CIFAR-10  for ResNet-20,-32,-44,-56,-110 (Table 2); On CIFAR-100 for ResNet-50(Table 14). On each of these datasets, we compare against 7 of the current state-of-art methods (including those suggested by the reviewers like DML and Guo et. al) and outperform these methods on the distillation task. 
In addition, we have added extensive ablation studies showing the regularization effect of adjoined training (Table 4). Again on several datasets and several models. 
---

### 2. Questions about the DAN loss function (Raised by reviewers 1 and 3)

We thank the reviewers for pointing out that the details of $n_f$ computation should be clarified for better understanding. We have modified the relevant section and added those details in the paper. Please refer to Section 5 for a more detailed discussion about the loss function. We provide more intuition and also explain it below. 

DAN uses architecture search (in our case searches over the possible values of alpha for the different layers of the network) to find the architecture that has the maximum accuracy. This is done by introducing a learnable parameter $\eta_i$ that combines the outputs of the different convolution filters for a particular layer (ref Fig 3 in the paper). As a simple example, consider a network with one convolution layer where the search space is three different values of $\alpha = \{1, 2, 4\}$. Then the final output of this layer will be $g(\eta_1) * conv(\alpha = 1)  + g(\eta_2) * conv(\alpha = 2) + g(\eta_3) * conv(\alpha = 4) $  (g is the gumbel function; details in Section 5 of the paper). At the end of DAN learning, we will use $\eta_1, \eta_2$ and $\eta_3$ to choose the value of $\alpha$ for this layer. Larger architectures tend to have higher accuracies. Hence the DAN learning tends to prefer networks with low alpha (larger architectures) to that with high alpha (smaller architectures). The $n_f$ term is added to the loss function as a penalty against DAN preferring large architectures. 

In case of the example layer above, $n_f = g(\eta_1) * n_{f1} + g(\eta_2) * n_{f2} + f(\eta_3) * n_{f3}$ where $n_{f1}$ measures the number of flops of the convolution layer corresponding to $\alpha = 1, n_{f2}$ corresponds to $\alpha = 2$ and $n_{f3}$ corresponds to $\alpha = 4$. Thus, the term $n_f$ is not a constant but depends on the parameter eta that is learned during DAN training. The same argument can be extended to larger networks.

Another point is regarding the large constant $\gamma$ in the loss function. Note that for a large network like ResNet-50, the number of flops corresponding to any setting of $\eta$’s can be very large. The term gamma normalizes it so that all the terms in the DAN loss function are in the same range.

content.title: A quick comment on the loss function
content.comment:
Since the discussion period ends on Nov 22nd, I'm leaving a quick comment on "DAN loss function", which I found as the most critical concern in my review below. I will write comments for other points later upon the authors' response to this comment.

I took a look at both Section 5 in the revision and comments here, but the concern on DAN loss function is still not resolved.
As commented in my first review below, it looks like **$n_f$ is NOT differentiable with respect to the input image $x$ (or inputs to intermediate layers either),
thus $\gamma \cdot n_f$ in Eq. (6) will be ignored when computing gradients of model parameters** while the authors call it a novel loss function.

This means, **as a loss function to optimize model parameters (by SGD, ADAM, etc), Eqs. (3) and (6) in the revision are essentially the same**.

Also, this is why I left this suggestion in my first review.

```
Suggestion: If the authors used Eq. 6 as metric for model selection  i.e., to choose which version of their (D)AN models should be used for evaluation, it should be re-formulated in a different way and referred to as an evaluation metric (for model selection) rather than a loss function optimized by SGD/Adam.
```

I'll be waiting for the authors' response to this comment.

content.title: Clarification on DAN loss function
content.comment:
Providing further clarification to the question. Let $L_1$ be the loss function as in Eqn. 3. This function depends on the input $x$ as well as the model parameters. When doing gradient descent using the $L_1$ loss function we are essentially solving the optimization problem $O_1$ where $$O_1 = \min_{\text{params}}   \sum_{x \in X}  L_1  (x,  \text{params} )  $$
where `params` denote the learnable parameters of our model (parameters for the conv layer, linear layer, batch norm etc) and $X$ denotes the training set. Now, let's denote the loss function in Eqn. 6 by $L_2$. Now, $L_2 = L_1 + \gamma . n_f$. If the optimization problem that we were solving were the following 
 $$O_2 = \min_{\text{params}}   \sum_{x \in X}  L_2  (x,  \text{params}, n_f )  =   \min_{\text{params}}  \sum_{x \in X} L_1  (x,  \text{params}) + \gamma . n_f $$
then we agree with the reviewer that $n_f$ is independent of `params`  and will be ignored by any optimization algorithm. I think this is where the confusion lies. In case of DAN we are not solving the optimization problem $O_2$ but the following optimization problem. 
$$O_3 = \min_{\text{params}, \eta }   \sum_{x \in X}  L_2  (x,  \text{params}, n_f )  =   \min_{\text{params}, \eta}  \sum_{x \in X} L_1  (x,  \text{params}) + \gamma . n_f (\eta )$$

In the view of the optimization problem $O_2$, we would first learn the model parameters using eqn. $L_1$ for different choices of $\alpha$ and then use eqn. $L_2$ as a model selection tool. This makes perfect sense and is an alternative approach for model selection and parameter tuning. But this is not what we are doing with the DAN loss function. 

The crucial novelty here is that in the optimization problem $O_3$, we are training from scratch and using Eqn. $L_2$ to simultaneously learn both $\eta$ (that will determine which value of $\alpha$ to use) and `params` (the model parameters of the different convolution layers, linear layer, etc).  In this case, the term $n_f$ will influence the values of $\eta$ and change with each iteration of gradient descent.

Another advantage of approach $O_3$ is that now we can optimize and search for different $\alpha$'s for different layers of the network. Thus, we can search over a much larger space ($3^{50}$ for a 50-layer network for example). https://towardsdatascience.com/what-is-gumbel-softmax-7f6d9cdcb90e (Bullet point #2).
